title: The Conversation as a Test: Golden Transcripts of a Device Session, and Ignoring Exactly What Should Differ

questions.question: Why record a whole session as a test instead of writing the expected value for each reply?
options: It needs no device, so it can replace the bench
It catches what a reply-at-a-time test misses
A recorded session is shorter than written expectations
It runs faster than a test of single replies
questions.explanation: A firmware change that adds a byte to every reply, or a reordering, and it is recorded and not composed. Each reply can look right by itself while the session as a whole has changed. And a recording is what the device really said, where an expectation is what someone thought it would.

questions.question: A transcript file has a line `> 0102`. What should the reader do?
options: Read it as two bytes, 01 and 02
Read it as one byte and ignore the rest
Refuse it: line 1, bytes are two hexadecimal digits each
Skip the line and read the others
questions.explanation: Two bytes with no space look like one number. Bytes are two hexadecimal digits each, separated by spaces. A reader that guessed would be comparing against something nobody wrote.

questions.question: Why does compare report only the first difference?
options: Later differences are slower to find
After the first one everything that follows is out of step, and a second report is noise
A test may only fail once
The transcript is read one line at a time
questions.explanation: Once one message differs in length or is missing, every later one is compared with the wrong partner. The first difference is the one that carries information.

questions.question: Replies carry a time of day at bytes 2 to 5 and it differs every run. What is the remedy?
options: A mask over exactly those bytes of replies
Compare only the lengths of the replies
Record the golden session again every day
Mask the whole of every reply
questions.explanation: Without it the first difference was message 1 byte 2, with it none. The time is the only thing allowed to change, so only those four bytes of replies are exempt. A mask over more than that would let real changes through.

questions.question: A mask covers bytes 2 to 5 of replies. A request's byte 1 and a reply's byte 6 are changed. What happens?
options: Both are caught: the mask covers only the direction and the bytes it was given for
Neither is caught: the mask hides them
Only the reply's byte 6 is caught
Only the request's byte 1 is caught
questions.explanation: The mask names a direction and a range of bytes. A request is the other direction and byte 6 is outside the range, so both are compared as usual.

questions.question: New firmware adds a byte to every reply. What does the golden transcript say?
options: Content, at message 0 byte 0
Extra, from message 6
Nothing: an added byte is ignored
Length, at message 1 and offset 8
questions.explanation: The first reply is longer and the shorter one ended at 8. The first reply is one byte longer than the golden one. That is reported as a difference in length, at the offset where the shorter message ended.
